latest_articles.title: “You Are a Mother, You Have to Suffer”: Communicative Resilience During Post-Cesarean Recovery Among Rural Bangladeshi Women
latest_articles.abstract: Research on post-cesarean recovery predominantly addresses physical healing, while less attention has been given to how women communicate pain, seek support, and manage family expectations during recovery, particularly in rural Bangladesh. Guided by the communication theory of resilience (CTR), this qualitative study examined how 20 women navigated recovery six to twelve months after cesarean birth. Semi-structured interviews conducted in Bengali were analyzed using applied thematic analysis. Findings were organized into two main themes: enduring fear, suffering, and silence; and enabling and constraining networks during postpartum recovery. Our study extends previous CTR research by showing how Bangladeshi women perform resilience during adverse and prolonged circumstances, in embodied ways that usurp-reinforce the gendered and patriarchal status quo on multiple levels, and by navigating profound social, material, and cultural constraints. Bangladeshi women coped with their circumstances through their mothers’ support and online networking. Like others who have experienced trauma, Bangladeshi mothers focused on ongoing productive adaptation to be able to survive. They felt encouraged by their digital networking through which they engaged in anticipatory resilience for more agentic possible futures and relational changes.

latest_articles.title: Disappearing Voices, Emerging Resistance: Journalism, Language, and Social Inequality in the U.S.-Mexico Borderlands
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how linguistic, geographic, and racial inequalities shape journalism in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Focusing on Southern Arizona, it analyzes the rise of two community-driven Spanish-language news startups following the closure of the city’s only Spanish-language newspaper. Emerging in connection with a bilingual journalism initiative at a local university, these projects developed through collaborative research, community engagement, and newsroom experimentation aimed at addressing gaps in local news coverage. Drawing on research-action practices, collaborative research, and self-ethnography, the study examines how marginalized communities resist exclusion by producing culturally relevant media. It situates these efforts within broader discussions of news deserts, institutional inequality, and the systemic neglect of linguistic minorities, offering insight into how grassroots journalism—and the institutional spaces that can help incubate it—can challenge dominant media norms and reimagine local news in underserved, multilingual communities.

latest_articles.title: A Mixed-Method Approach to Exploring the Role of Strategic Internal Communication in Fostering Employee Passion at Work
latest_articles.abstract: This mixed-method study explores how strategic internal communication in the organization can foster employee passion at work. Drawing on interviews with 23 internal communication leaders and a national survey of 1,014 full-time U.S. employees, the study identifies key communication strategies such as purpose communication, openness, empathy, and participation that influences passion. Quantitative analysis reveals that dialogic communication and purpose communication both significantly enhance employee passion, with sense of meaningfulness mediating these effects. Rich communication channels, especially face-to-face and digital media, emerged as the most effective in fostering employee passion at work. This study offers both theoretical and practical insights, advancing the internal communication and workplace passion literature and providing actionable guidance for communication professionals.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

latest_articles.title: Innovation Narratives in Startups: Legitimation Grammars Under Inequality in Brazilian and International Technology Ventures
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how technology startups communicatively construct and legitimate their innovation activities through organizational narratives. Drawing on the Communicative Constitution of Organizations perspective, organizational narrative theory, and legitimation studies, we analyse publicly circulating self-descriptions from twelve technology ventures spanning fintech, logistics, creator economy, e-commerce, proptech, healthtech, foodtech, mobility and B2B SaaS. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we identify five narrative types (Disruption, Inclusion, Growth, Impact, and Team/Founder) and five articulation patterns. The central finding concerns narrative position rather than presence: Inclusion Narratives occupy dominant positions in the majority of ventures operating within inequality-dense institutional environments, while appearing exclusively as secondary narratives in ventures embedded in mature capital markets. We interpret this asymmetry as a re-specification of legitimation grammars conditioned by structural inequality, financial exclusion, and historical underprovision of services. The study contributes an empirically grounded contextual qualification of disruption-centred accounts of entrepreneurial legitimation, a typology of narrative articulation patterns, and an initial theorization of the Infrastructural Narrative as a legitimation strategy in platform economies.
affiliations: Centro Universitário Adventista de São Paulo (UNASP)

latest_articles.title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
latest_articles.abstract: Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.
affiliations: Flinders University Institute for Mental Health and Wellbeing, College of Human Sciences and Culture, Flinders University, Adelaide, SA, Australia

latest_articles.title: Cross-platformization: How U.S. right-leaning media curate their posts on Twitter and Truth Social
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

latest_articles.title: Being journalists on social media: Contrasting professionals’ self-perceptions to role expectations among adolescents
latest_articles.abstract: On social media, efforts by individual journalists to share news with audiences may be a viable response to personality-driven news presentation coming from peripheral actors like influencers, who are increasingly popular information sources for adolescents. Yet, when using social media to disseminate content, journalists may risk backlash, especially when innovative approaches represent a deviation from traditional journalistic norms. Drawing on expectancy violations theory and semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted among Portuguese journalists ( N = 7) and adolescents ( N = 20), we contrasted professionals’ own perceptions of being journalists on social media to adolescents’ role expectations. Findings showed that adolescents generally prefer journalists to be personal and independent when presenting news on social media, though they also recognized that journalists may in this context be bound by institutional rules. Similarly, journalists highlighted perceived pressure coming from news organizations and licensing bodies to abide by professional standards, even when using their private social media. Despite seeing value in adopting a ‘newsfluencer’-like role, journalists’ need to negotiate between various interests and expectations represents one of the main hurdles that prevents them from establishing a clear presence on these platforms – and may explain low attraction to journalistic sources on social media among adolescents.

latest_articles.title: When even empathy would be enough – Representation of homelessness in the Czech mainstream media during Christmas
latest_articles.abstract: Homelessness remains one of the most persistent and complex societal issues globally, and the media play a significant role in shaping both representations of and public attitudes toward this marginalized population. This study presents a thematic analysis of Czech mainstream news coverage of homelessness during three consecutive Christmas periods (2022, 2023, and 2024). While Christmas coverage might be expected to foreground empathy, humanization, or solidarity more strongly than routine reporting, the analysis shows that such elements remained relatively marginal in the Czech material examined here. The findings reveal a persistent scarcity of solidarity and empathy, with media portrayals frequently reinforcing harmful stereotypes rather than challenging them. The study concludes that substantial changes in media discourse are necessary to promote more accurate and just representations of homelessness in the Czech and possibly further Eastern European context.

latest_articles.title: Pressured by the Comments? Chinese Journalists in the Face of Online Violence
latest_articles.abstract: In the increasingly digital context of China’s public sphere, journalists frequently encounter online violence that threatens their professional autonomy, emotional wellbeing, and freedom of expression. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with journalists representing a cross section of the Chinese media landscape, this study identifies four major types of online violence experienced by Chinese journalists: violence in response to alleged unprofessional behaviours, violence based on moral coercion, violence motivated by so-called “nationalism”, and gendered violence. Cultural norms, nationalist ideologies, and patriarchy emerge as key factors shaping and underpinning online violence. With regard to journalists’ coping strategies, these are found to include individualised and emotionally taxing approaches, such as silence, avoidance and contempt, while institutional support is either limited in its responsiveness or sometimes unavailable. This study provides an enhanced understanding of the role of online violence in shaping journalistic practice and coping strategies in a highly interactive and emotional digital media environment. The findings indicate that online violence driven by wider structural and cultural forces, is becoming an increasingly common informal control mechanism, undermining journalistic authority and autonomy and therefore the stability and sustainability of journalism itself.

latest_articles.title: Worldviews and public attitudes toward gene-edited foods in Japan
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines public attitudes toward gene-edited foods in Japan, focusing on how underlying worldviews shape these responses. Drawing on a national survey and a latent class segmentation model based on 23 worldview variables, we identify four distinct segments: Communitarian, Environmentalist, Governmentalist, and Individualist. The findings indicate modest rather than sharply polarized differences in attitudes, with the Communitarian and Environmentalist segments expressing greater caution than the Governmentalist and Individualist segments. Across all four segments, gene-edited foods are broadly perceived as unnatural, yet support for commercialization remains comparatively high, suggesting that perceptions of unnaturalness do not necessarily translate into strong opposition to commercialization. This pattern suggests that evaluations of gene-edited foods are shaped by multiple normative considerations, in which moral or symbolic concerns coexist with pragmatic judgments about societal benefits and technological governance. These findings suggest that similar levels of support or skepticism can emerge from differing normative orientations.
affiliations: College of Liberal Arts, International Christian University, Tokyo, Japan

latest_articles.title: A Causal Inference on the Effects of Attention to Media Content About Autonomous Vehicles in the Influence of Presumed Media Influence Model
latest_articles.abstract: Applying the influence of presumed media influence model into an autonomous vehicle (AV) context, this study examines how media viewers’ attention to content about risks and benefits of AVs affects their presumptions of influence of the content on others, perceptions of trustworthiness of the technology, and intention to ride in AVs. Through cross-lagged analyses of two-wave panel data (n wave1 = 1,306; n wave2 = 650), this study found causal evidence for the projection effect and impersonal impact. Notably, this study also found causal evidence for the consonance effect: viewers perceiving trustworthiness of AVs after developing intention to ride in AVs.

latest_articles.title: Investigating Conditional Macro-Level Media Effects Over a Long-Term: How Crisis Periods Moderate the Effects of Suicide Coverage on Suicide Rate Change (1861–2007)
latest_articles.abstract: How does media shape society over decades, and does its effect vary depending on the societal atmosphere or zeitgeist ? While theoretically important, there is a lack of systematic empirical evidence on conditional long-term macro-level media effects. We propose a broader framework to study such effects and demonstrate its applicability for the “Werther effect” in the UK. More specifically, we investigate whether media coverage of suicides in a newspaper of record is linked to suicide rates and whether this link changes during societal crises. For this, we combine suicide data with a large-scale automated content analysis of crisis and suicide reporting in The Times over a century (1861-2007). Our analysis shows that increased suicide reporting is associated with higher suicide rates, but only during crisis periods. The results are consistent with a conditional Werther effect and may offer one piece of the larger puzzle of long-term macro-level media influences on society.
affiliations: GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne, Germany

latest_articles.title: Structural Media Capture: Rethinking media in the Global South
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops Structural Media Capture (SMC) as a theoretical framework for rethinking media power in postcolonial settings. Challenging the universalization of liberal-democratic normative models of the press, it advances a de-Westernizing approach that situates media development within historically specific institutional trajectories rather than universal ideals. The article theorizes from Morocco, with comparative reference to the Arab media context, and identifies three overlapping configurations of capture: post-independence state consolidation, market-driven economic dependency, and platform-based infrastructural control. Its central claim is that these configurations interact and accumulate, producing a layered architecture of media constraint. SMC does more than aggregate accounts of political, economic, or platform domination. It reconceptualizes media capture as a path-dependent and multi-level formation through which older regimes of control persist within newer institutional arrangements. In doing so, the article offers a historically grounded grammar for comparative media theory and proposes a framework for analysis across Global South contexts.
affiliations: College of Communication, University of Sharjah , Sharjah,

latest_articles.title: Digital ID as surreptitious experimentation in the humanitarian-tech industry: an ethnography of a biometric pilot in a refugee camp in the Thailand-Myanmar border
latest_articles.abstract: This article focuses on a technological pilot involving a digital identity system that was introduced in the hospital of a refugee camp along the Thailand-Myanmar border. Drawing on an 18-month-long ethnographic study of refugees’ experiences with biometric systems, the article analyses the pilot as an example of ‘surreptitious experimentation’. Surreptitious experimentation is symptomatic of the wider commercialisation and digital infrastructuring of the humanitarian space, which we make sense of through the term ‘humanitarian-tech industry’. This is a mixed methods study involving semi-structured and group interviews, participatory art sessions and ethnography. In total, we spoke with 174 refugees and 27 expert participants involved in the aid operations. The research found that the digital ID system was implemented despite local misgivings. The term ‘surreptitious’ illustrates the fact that the new system was not announced as a ‘pilot’, but rather simply rolled out to replace existing forms of patient registration. Because the pilot took place in the infrastructural background, it remained hidden. The article documents the lack of local understanding and meaningful consent among refugees. The promise of ‘self-sovereign’ decentralised identity advocated by the pilot sponsors was never communicated to the local communities, let alone ever realised, even when a need for data portability emerged. Instead, the article observes that the pilot introduced harms and amplified the asymmetries which already exist in humanitarian and particularly medical humanitarian settings. As an exemplar of surreptitious experimentation, the digital ID pilot reworked and revitalised the colonial logics of aid.

latest_articles.title: Facebook as a Lifeboat: An Interview Study Exploring the Role of Facebook in Supporting Parents of Children with Rare Diseases
latest_articles.abstract: Parents of children with rare diseases face unique challenges due to scarce medical expertise and limited information sources. Social media, particularly Facebook, have become a vital (and sometimes the only) space for parents to access information, share experiences, and find emotional support. This study examined how parents of children with an ultra-rare genetic condition [FOXP1] engage with a Facebook group. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 19 parents across eight countries and analyzed using thematic analysis. Based on the results, we developed the “Phased Social Media Engagement in Rare Disease Caregiving” model. The model illustrates how informational, emotional, and psychological needs may vary across the caregiving journey and under different circumstances. This model delineates three phases of engagement: (1) Frantic, characterized by intensive information seeking and urgent reassurance seeking commonly described around the time of diagnosis; (2) Selective and Saturated, in which parents, having surpassed an information threshold, used Facebook more strategically for targeted problem-solving and advocacy, while consciously avoiding distressing content; and (3) Mentoring, in which some parents guided and reassured newly diagnosed families, deriving meaning and identity through supporting others. Results highlight both the benefits and risks of online peer support groups, underscoring the need for healthcare providers to acknowledge these groups and help parents navigate information overload and emotional triggers.
affiliations: Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Ghent University

latest_articles.title: “I Am Allowed to Cough Here”: How Icon and Audience Characteristics Affect the Comprehension of Covid-19 Icons in the Netherlands and Flanders
latest_articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic challenged Dutch and Flemish municipalities to provide clear, understandable instructions about preventive measures. Each municipality designed its own icons to convey these preventive measures. We conducted two studies to examine both the characteristics of these icons and their comprehension by the public. First, a content analysis revealed a predominance of instructional over prohibitive icons, and many did not contain text. More concrete and dynamic icons were semantically closer to the intended message, while those with text tended to be visually complex. Second, we tested the comprehension of eight icons among Dutch and Flemish citizens. Results indicated that three of the icons did not meet ISO-standard for comprehension. Perceived clarity turned out the be the strongest predictor of accurate interpretation. Additionally, lower education levels and non-native language backgrounds were associated with higher rates of misunderstanding. Misinterpretations were linked to color choice, complexity, and visual salience. Together, these findings provide insights for designing clear and effective visual instructions to support public understanding during health crises.

latest_articles.title: Beyond Amplifiers and Watchdogs: Rethinking Institutional Science Communication–Journalism Relations in Hybrid Media Ecosystems
latest_articles.abstract: Contemporary science communication increasingly unfolds within hybrid media ecosystems where scientists, institutional communicators, journalists, and audiences interact under rapidly changing conditions. In these ecosystems, universities and other research organisations have become highly visible communicative actors, supported by growing investments in strategic science communication. At the same time, science journalism faces economic precarity, shrinking newsroom capacity, and growing reliance on institutional sources. These developments have fuelled long-standing debates about hype, churnalism, and the erosion of journalism’s watchdog function, often framed as ethical or professional failings. However, these tensions between institutional science communicators and science journalists can also be seen as the structural consequences of contemporary science communication rather than as interpersonal conflicts or normative shortcomings. We conceptualise this relationship through two analytical lenses. A high-tension perspective foregrounds risks to journalistic independence, critical scrutiny, the watchdog role, and public trust under conditions of media asymmetry and the expansion of institutional authority over the public communication of science. A low-tension perspective highlights functional interdependence, role complementarity, and the ways institutional communication can enable science journalism in constrained media environments. Rather than treating these perspectives as competing accounts, we use them to illuminate different normative stakes within the same ecosystem. We thus propose a framework for constructive interdependence that acknowledges blurred boundaries and role overlap while actively protecting the integrity of independent scrutiny, and argue that safeguarding journalism’s watchdog role should be understood as a shared responsibility across communicators, institutions, and intermediaries. While we wrote this piece primarily for science communication scholars, we hope that the proposed framework offers science journalists, institutional science communicators, and research funders four concrete principles for protecting independent scrutiny as science communication ecosystems continue to change.

latest_articles.title: Scientific Watchdog Journalism in Latin America: A Challenge of Broken Mirrors
latest_articles.abstract: The watchdog role of science journalism, as a way of revealing wrongdoings in science-driven enterprises, is a recent and rather invisible practice in Latin America. From my 20 years as a practitioner, this commentary explores some structural causes of this phenomenon: insufficient training opportunities in science journalism; a weak perspective of the watchdog role; a cheerleader posture by the media towards science; symbolic and political links between media owners and scientific elites; and the vulnerable position of journalists due to fragile incomes, which compromises independence and critical thinking. I also underline a further watchdog role: to investigate, expose, and warn society about the misuses and abuses of scientific methods, processes, outcomes, and authority in the public domain. In this role, the watchdog journalist verifies scientific arguments invoked to make decisions. Lastly, I relate successful instances of watchdog science journalism in the region for the social evaluation of scientific knowledge and its impact on urgent Global South problems.

latest_articles.title: Threat and Remedy: AI’s Technological and Normative Role in Democratic Discourse and Counter Speech
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed online discourse, serving simultaneously as a source of and a potential solution to threats to democracy. This article conceptually examines AI’s multifaceted role in digital public spheres, beginning with an analysis of how AI shapes democratic processes online, ranging from information curation and political participation to dialogue facilitation and the construction of epistemic infrastructures. We identify several key risks: AI amplifies harmful content through automated content generation, coordinated manipulation, and the algorithmic mainstreaming of borderline content that often evades traditional detection systems. Within this broader democratic context, we position counter speech as a critical intervention strategy and examine both reactive measures (e.g., automated detection and content moderation) and proactive approaches (e.g., prebunking, algorithmic downranking, friction design, and AI-mediated dialogue). We argue that effective counter speech increasingly relies on human–AI collaboration, where AI supports human counter speakers with factual resources, emotional scaffolding, and scalability, while human actors preserve the authenticity and agency that make counter speech normatively meaningful. However, realizing the potential of such collaboration requires moving beyond technological fixes toward democratically legitimated governance structures. Drawing on examples from Wikipedia and decentralized platforms, we demonstrate how transparent and participatory institutional arrangements can foster more resilient discourse environments. We conclude that societies can harness AI’s democratic potential while mitigating its risks only by proactively establishing legitimate deliberative processes grounded in broadly shared discourse norms.

latest_articles.title: Spillover and Crossover Effects of Financial Stress in Romantic Dyads: A Daily Diary Study
latest_articles.abstract: Financial stress can strain romantic relations through stress spillover (affecting oneself) and crossover (affecting one's partner). This study investigated how financial stress influences relationship stress and the role of dyadic coping strategies. Eighty‐four unmarried US couples ( N = 168 respondents) completed a one‐time baseline assessment and a 7‐day daily diary reporting financial stress, relationship stress, and perceived dyadic coping. Multilevel modeling showed financial stress significantly predicted both one's own and one's partner's relationship stress at baseline. Emotion‐focused dyadic coping (providing support, reassurance) buffered this association, whereas problem‐focused coping had no buffering effect and may even worsen stress spillover. Daily analyses revealed that financial stress and relationship stress covary over time, especially for couples with high baseline relationship stress. These findings underscore the protective role of emotion‐focused dyadic coping in managing immediate relational strain due to financial stress, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to foster relationship resilience in financially vulnerable couples.
affiliations: Department of Psychology University of Florida Gainesville Florida USA

latest_articles.title: Testing the Extrinsic Convergent Validity of Relationship Quality Constructs
latest_articles.abstract: Relationship scientists have developed a rich array of constructs to describe the quality of relationships. Yet, questions have emerged regarding the validity of these constructs. Building on these questions, we examine the validity of a set of core constructs in relationship science. Specifically, we use extrinsic convergent validity testing to assess the extent to which the six components of the perceived relationship quality components measure (PRQC) represent distinct constructs in predicting self‐reported behavior within romantic relationships. Across one between‐subjects study ( N = 601) and one within‐subjects study ( N = 603), we used multiple indices of heterogeneity, structural equation modeling, and factor analysis to demonstrate the utility of extrinsic convergent validity testing and illustrate that some components of the PRQC appear to uniquely predict relationship behavior, whereas others may not. Implications and future directions are discussed, with particular emphasis placed on refining both measurement and theory practices.

latest_articles.title: Disclosure and supportive communication patterns in the cancer pre-diagnosis phase
latest_articles.abstract: Health-related disclosure decisions can be a source of both distress and social support. Using Greene’s Disclosure Decision-Making Model (DD-MM) as the theoretical framework, this research assesses disclosure and support needs of individuals within the cancer pre-diagnosis phase (i.e. undergoing advanced testing for cancer due to troubling symptoms). Fifty-five participants who had undergone a cancer diagnosis experience within the last 5 years were interviewed about their social support needs during the cancer pre-diagnosis phase. The pre-diagnosis phase is unique in the disease trajectory because extensive uncertainties remain surrounding symptom causes, diagnosis, and prognosis. Through thematic analysis, two macro-level themes were identified focused on selective disclosure and social support. Subthemes, including testing unawareness or denial, a unique form of pre-diagnosis stigma, letting the patient set the tone, and support preferences from similar peers, are developed within. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how the DD-MM operates under diagnostic uncertainty, where minimal health information reshapes all three factors of the model. This research also offers practical advice for pre-diagnosis patients, supporters, and healthcare providers.

latest_articles.title: Double Adaptation: Negotiating Closeness and Managing Boundaries in Journalist–Politician Relations
latest_articles.abstract: Closeness with politicians is both a professional resource and a potential risk for journalists, as it enables access to information but may compromise autonomy and integrity, particularly within today’s hybrid media environment. This study proposes the conceptual framework of double adaptation as a sensitizing, process-oriented lens for a more systematic understanding of how journalists manage boundaries with politicians, drawing on 96 semi-structured interviews with political journalists in Austria and Czechia. Double adaptation captures the dual process through which journalists adjust their practices in response to both immediate situational demands and structural conditions. Boundaries in journalist–politician interactions emerge through situational adaptation to specific contexts, requiring a careful balancing across multiple dimensions of closeness. The analysis identifies nine such dimensions, grouped into two domains: interactions and relationships. The study further identifies individual factors shaping situational adaptation, including symbolic and pragmatic approaches to boundary management, and situational factors such as personal affinity. Simultaneously, boundaries result from structural adaptation operating at organizational, professional, and systemic levels, influenced by digital transformation, economic pressures, and the professionalization of political communication. Together, these insights advance a more systematic and processual conceptualization of boundary management in political journalism by linking everyday interactional practices to broader structural transformations.

latest_articles.title: From Policy to Personal Wellness: Identifying Health Journalism Beats by Specialty Topic and Journalist Characteristics
latest_articles.abstract: Health journalists provide essential, verified information on a range of topics including wellness, medical research, health policy, and health business. We conducted a national online survey of US health journalists (N = 629) to investigate how occupational practices and perceptions vary for health journalists who specialize in different health topics. Latent class analysis identified four distinct health beats: personal health and wellness, health sciences and research, health business, and health systems. The four beats are associated with variations in how journalists frame stories, the reach of the outlets they work for, whether they are staff or freelancers, how much of their reporting work is about health, as well as their job satisfaction and autonomy to choose topics and frame stories. Comparing health beats highlights distinctions in how health journalists consider health beyond the individual level, including public health, social determinants of health, and health policy, and how local journalists differ from national health journalists in their emphasis on health systems, health policy, and other issues of immediate relevance for communities.

latest_articles.title: Shut Your Eyes in the Dark! Differential Effects of Pre-Bedtime and Pre-Shuteye Media Use on Sleep Delay and Anxiety
latest_articles.abstract: The pervasive use of digital media before sleep is increasingly recognized as a critical factor affecting sleep and psychological well-being. However, the impact of bedtime media at different stages-specifically, before bedtime and before shuteye-remains unclear. Using data from the United Kingdom Time Use Survey collected between 2016 and 2021, this study analyzes 3,044 diary entries from 1,577 adults aged 18-45, aiming to investigate the relationship between bedtime media use, sleep delay, and anxiety. Results indicate that pre-shuteye media use significantly delays sleep and increases anxiety, while pre-bedtime media use does not delay sleep but is directly associated with reduced anxiety. Notably, as a key mechanism through which digital media use impacts anxiety, both bedtime and shuteye time reflect delayed sleep, with shuteye time playing the primary role. This study contributes to our understanding of shuteye time as a mechanism in media effects, shedding light on the source of anxiety among adults.

latest_articles.title: “Intimacy at a Distance” in Later Life: Parasocial Relationship and Its Associations with Loneliness and Well-Being Among Older Adults
latest_articles.abstract: Loneliness among older adults is a growing public health concern, given its close association with their overall well-being. Drawing on the social surrogacy hypothesis, which suggests that parasocial relationship (PSR) can provide a sense of belonging and social connection, this study examined whether PSR is indirectly associated with subjective well-being through different dimensions of loneliness among older adults. Specifically, we adopted a multidimensional perspective on loneliness by distinguishing among family, romantic, and social loneliness. We also investigated whether these indirect associations would be moderated by gender. Using cross-sectional survey data from 934 adults aged 60 and over in South Korea, we found that PSR was indirectly associated with positive affect and life satisfaction through romantic and social loneliness. Notably, the indirect effects of PSR on positive affect and life satisfaction through social loneliness varied by gender, such that these effects were significant for older men but not for older women. These findings extend the social surrogacy hypothesis to understanding PSR's role in older adults' loneliness and well-being.

latest_articles.title: The Limits and Levers of Influence: What Works in Alcohol Harm-Reduction Campaigns
latest_articles.abstract: Alcohol harm-reduction campaigns are widely used, yet rarely produce sustained behavioral change. Synthesizing evidence from 116 studies, this article explains why campaigns often shift awareness and attitudes but fail to translate these effects into action. It introduces a Limits and Levers framework identifying four mechanisms shaping effectiveness: alignment (message-audience fit), psychological activation (emotion, efficacy, resistance), social amplification (norms, peer diffusion), and structural integration (media and environmental conditions). Findings show that campaigns underperform when designed as standalone efforts. Effectiveness increases when communication is embedded in broader systems of influence. This perspective shifts focus from whether campaigns work to how they work in practice.
affiliations: The John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin

latest_articles.title: Editorial: Automating Trust: AI, Misinformation, and the Future of Algorithmic Fact-Checking
latest_articles.abstract: This special issue editorial introduces “Automating Trust: AI, Misinformation, and the Future of Algorithmic Fact-Checking,” examining how AI-driven verification systems reshape trust, accuracy, and authority in public discourse. Opening with a case where an AI system flagged authentic content over a misleading caption, the editorial frames algorithmic fact-checking as carrying its own biases even as it offers speed and scale beyond human capacity. The twenty collected papers—spanning surveys, experiments, interviews, and computational analysis across the US, Singapore, China, South Korea, and the Arabic-speaking world—explore political effects, audience trust, disclosure practices, organizational dynamics, and correction strategies. Recurring themes include the primacy of provenance and transparency over AI’s mere presence, tension between efficiency and human judgment, and trust in AI verification as inseparable from trust in surrounding institutions.

latest_articles.title: Algorithms and ABCs: Associations between US parents’ educational media motivations and content quality on YouTube
latest_articles.abstract: YouTube usage among young children is highly prevalent, but prior content analyses suggest that YouTube contains substantial amounts of low educational content. We examined associations between parental motivations to use media to educate, child YouTube usage, and educational content of YouTube videos viewed. We also examined associations between educational content of YouTube videos and presence of educational claims in the video title or channel name. Using surveys from 286 parents of 2-year-olds, parents were classified as having low, moderate, or high motivation to use media to educate, and YouTube videos from 133 participants were coded for educational content. Parents in the high-motivation group were significantly more likely than the low-motivation group to report regular child YouTube viewing. Parents’ educational motivation was not significantly associated with the educational quality of videos their child watched in terms of mean scores or proportion of high-quality videos. Presence of educational claims in the title or channel name was not significantly different between videos of low or high educational quality. Despite parents’ best intentions, there may be other factors impacting the quality of media that children are watching on YouTube.
affiliations: University of Michigan School of Public Health

latest_articles.title: Selfies as a tool for self-presentation: Relations between strategic selfie-behavior, peer feedback and appearance dis/satisfaction among Belgian teens
latest_articles.abstract: Taking and posting selfies is one of the most popular activities adolescents engage in on social media. This study explored how different types of selfie practices (i.e. selfie investment and editing) relate to appearance dissatisfaction. Across two cross-sectional studies, Belgian adolescents (Study 1: N = 806, age range = 13–19 years; Mage = 15.58; Study 2: N = 262, age range = 13–19 years; Mage = 15.99) reported on their self-presentation expectancies, selfie practices, body surveillance, appearance dissatisfaction, and selfie feedback (positive and negative). Results revealed that both selfie investment and selfie editing were positively related to appearance dissatisfaction, though through different mechanisms. Selfie editing elicited more negative feedback and diminished positive responses, escalating appearance dissatisfaction. Conversely, selfie investment was positively associated with both positive feedback – buffering against appearance dissatisfaction – and body surveillance, which exacerbates appearance dissatisfaction. These insights underscore the nuanced impact of different selfie behaviors on body image, suggesting varied mechanisms that may explain their connection to body image concerns.

latest_articles.title: The meaning of ‘normal’ – children’s negotiation of (normal) masculinity, femininity, and LGBTQ media representations in Flanders
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how 55 children (aged 10–12) in Flanders interpret LGBTQ media representations and negotiate related norms of gender and sexuality. Drawing on twelve focus groups across four different schools, the research investigates the dynamics of their peer interactions, focusing on how meanings were affirmed, contested, and redefined. The findings reveal the dominance of respect and inclusion as social norms, while also highlighting the ambivalence that underlies children’s discussions. Although “respect” was consistently articulated as the appropriate response, it often functioned as a floating signifier, expressed within heteronormative and cultural boundaries. Heterosexuality was frequently framed as “normal”, while LGBTQ identities were positioned as “different” or “unusual”. Four thematic clusters emerged: hegemonic masculinity, negotiable femininity, transgender identities, and ethno-cultural contexts. Boys, in particular, were constrained by peer norms regulating acceptable masculinity, while girls tended to respond with greater reflection. Children from minority ethno-cultural backgrounds often articulated ambivalent views, reflecting the interplay of religious beliefs, family expectations, and school norms. This study shows that LGBTQ inclusion does not automatically translate into unambiguous acceptance among younger generations, even in contexts where legal protections for minority groups are well established.

latest_articles.title: Factors Influencing Wearable Technology Adoption
latest_articles.abstract: As wearable health technologies become increasingly important in preventive healthcare and personal health management, understanding the factors that drive user adoption has become a critical issue for researchers and practitioners. Although previous studies have examined wearable technology adoption from either health-related or technology-related perspectives, limited research has integrated these perspectives within a comprehensive framework. This study develops an integrated framework based on the Health Belief Model (HBM), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and self-efficacy to investigate factors influencing users' attitudes and intentions toward wearable health devices. Data were collected via an online survey of 385 Taiwanese adults, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to test the proposed relationships. Results show that perceived health threat, perceived usefulness, and self-efficacy significantly influence user attitudes, which in turn affect behavioral intention, while perceived ease of use exerts an indirect effect. Barriers such as low perceived need and limited technological confidence were identified as adoption inhibitors. The findings indicate that both health-related perceptions and technology-related evaluations jointly influence wearable technology adoption decisions. The findings provide an integrated framework that combines health belief and technology acceptance perspectives, offering practical implications for healthcare communicators, technology developers, marketers, and policymakers to enhance user engagement, improve device design, and promote preventive health behaviors through wearable healthcare technologies.

latest_articles.title: Using Diffusion of Innovations Theory to Predict Engagement with Healthy Recipe Posts in Social Media
latest_articles.abstract: = 300), participants in online surveys viewed one social media post (randomly selected from larger pools) promoting a healthy recipe. After viewing the social media post, participants rated their intention to click on the link, make the recipe, and share the recipe post then rated that recipe on four DOI theory attributes: relative advantage, compatibility with their lifestyle, complexity, and trialability. In each study, Ordinary Least Squares regression was used to examine the relationship between DOI theory attributes and each intention measure. Results consistently demonstrated that a recipe's perceived relative advantage and perceived compatibility were significant predictors of intention to click on, make, or share the recipe. Complexity and trialability were rarely significant predictors of intentions. These results can be used to inform both message development and message testing strategies for nutrition-focused campaigns, as nutrition interventions that are seen as being higher in relative advantage and compatibility may be more readily adopted by priority populations.

latest_articles.title: Theorizing Intercultural Communication Through Dimensional Accrual and Dissociation
latest_articles.abstract: This paper elaborates the theory of dimensional accrual and dissociation (DAD) as an approach to intercultural communication research, offering novelty towards the framing of difference. DAD provides an alternative to traditional structural-functional theories, which frequently treat culture as an external communicative feature rather than an ontology. Accordingly, traditional approaches imply that culture and difference are obstacles to be overcome instead of normal, valuable elements of communication itself. In place of functionalism, DAD draws on multidisciplinarity to posit that intercultural communication is framed by different awarenesses of the world – architectures of consciousness – which enable an array of rich, complex communicative activities.

latest_articles.title: The disappearance of a Chinese village: How short-video platforms mediatized Clifftop Village’s lifeworld
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how the secluded Clifftop Village rapidly transitioned from a pre-digital society into a mediatized world via short-video platforms. Drawing on fieldwork and interviews, we find that mediatization in this media-deprived rural community was triggered by an incidental news report and unfolded along leapfrogging trajectories driven by the marginalized group’s short-video practices. This process stemmed from complex negotiations between structural forces—China’s centralized governance, expanding digital infrastructure, and platform capital—and the agency of marginalized subjects. It systematically reconfigured villagers’ spatio-temporal order, social relationships, cultural beliefs, and lifestyles, ultimately precipitating the complete relocation of the entire community. Following the dissolution of the physical community, mediatization extended into the affective realm, as villagers began to rely on short-video platforms to anchor their sense of place and collective identity. Ultimately, the case of Clifftop Village demonstrates that rural mediatization cannot be reduced to either technological empowerment or the reproduction of digital inequality, offering a localized lens on the existential condition of marginalized groups under radical modernization.

latest_articles.title: Inequality Within the Mobile System: Understanding the Third-Level Digital Divide Through Adverse Digital Incorporation in Rural China
latest_articles.abstract: As mobile media rapidly expand in the rural Global South, digital divide research is shifting from an exclusion-based to an inclusion-based perspective. Drawing on Heeks’ “adverse digital incorporation” framework and ethnographic fieldwork in rural China, this article conceptualizes the third-level digital divide, which refers to the unequal outcomes and disparate dividends derived from information and communication technologies, as the unequal extraction of value resulting from power imbalances within the mobile system. The study reveals that this adverse incorporation constitutes two closed loops of value inequality. On the one hand, smartphones break spatiotemporal boundaries to extract value through the commodification of private time, legibility and labor control, and risk-cost shifting. On the other hand, while rural residents employ strategic digital disconnection as a form of everyday resistance, which results in marginalization and reinforces value inequality. Consequently, it is essential to go beyond technical provision to enable rural residents to transform from passive content consumers into active value producers and to rebalance power within the mobile system.
affiliations: National Center for Cultural Innovation Research, Fudan University, Shanghai, China

latest_articles.title: Experimental Research on Stereotype Expression in Freely Generated Language: A Systematic Literature Review
latest_articles.abstract: Social stereotypes spread through biased language. Experiments in which participants freely generate language allow researchers to causally test how stereotypes affect language use and capture multiple linguistic variables simultaneously, offering high ecological validity. Despite this potential, it remains unclear how and to which extent this paradigm has been used to study linguistic biases. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review ( k = 106 experiments) and found that most freely generated language experiments examined only one linguistic variable, leaving the interplay between linguistic variables largely underexplored. To advance our understanding of stereotype expression in everyday language, we recommend experiments to measure multiple linguistic variables simultaneously and in relation to each other. This knowledge is needed to address harmful stereotype communication in the real world through automated detection tools, communication interventions, and the fine-tuning of Large Language Models.

latest_articles.title: Relationship Between Cyberbullying and Social Anxiety, School Refusal, and Academic Goals in Adolescents
latest_articles.abstract: Examining the associations between cyberbullying involvement and psychoeducational factors may contribute to a better understanding of adolescents’ experiences in online peer contexts. The aim of this study was to examine the associations between cyberbullying involvement, considering the roles of cybervictim, cyberaggressor, and cyberbystander, and three psychoeducational constructs: social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. A total of 1,412 Spanish secondary and upper-secondary school students aged 12–18 years ( M = 14.36, SD = 1.65) completed a battery of questionnaires assessing cyberbullying, social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. Three independent binary logistic regression models were conducted, one for each cyberbullying role, using the psychoeducational dimensions as predictors. The findings showed that the associations varied according to both the psychoeducational dimension and the cyberbullying role. In particular, Discomfort and avoidance in social situations in general was positively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas other dimensions of social anxiety showed negative associations with some roles. Avoidance of stimuli or situations related to the school context was positively associated with the three cyberbullying roles. Learning and Achievement goals were negatively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas Social reinforcement goals were positively associated with cyberaggression. These findings highlight the multidimensional nature of the associations between psychoeducational factors and cyberbullying involvement and support the consideration of individual and educational variables in the design of prevention and intervention strategies during adolescence.

latest_articles.title: Bibliometric mapping of intercultural competence research in Web of Science (2015–2024): A CiteSpace analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Intercultural competence is widely recognized as a key capability for effective communication across cultural boundaries in an increasingly globalized world. This study employs bibliometric analysis and CiteSpace to map the intellectual structure, thematic development, and emerging trends of intercultural competence research indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) from 2015 to 2024. Drawing on a dataset of 1319 English-language journal articles, the analysis examines publication trends, identifies active countries, influential authors and journals, and explores research hotspots and emerging directions through keyword co-occurrence, clustering, and burst analyses. The findings reveal substantial growth in WoS-indexed intercultural competence research over the past decade, with the United States, China, and the United Kingdom playing leading roles in knowledge production and international collaboration. Major research domains include intercultural competence and education, internationalization, professional development, and technology-mediated intercultural learning. Emerging trends indicate increasing scholarly attention to virtual exchange, workplace applications of intercultural competence, and digitally supported intercultural interaction. In addition, a qualitative interpretive reading of influential works highlights enduring conceptual tensions concerning the nature, assessment, and application of intercultural competence across contexts. This study provides an updated overview of the development of intercultural competence research within the WoS-indexed literature and identifies key directions for future inquiry. The findings offer valuable insights for educators, policymakers, and researchers seeking to promote intercultural competence in educational, professional, and digitally mediated environments.

latest_articles.title: Comparing the intercultural sensitivity of American tertiary faculty abroad and domestically: A case for contextual consideration in assessing sensitivity
latest_articles.abstract: This qualitative study establishes and compares the Intercultural Sensitivity (IS) of tertiary American faculty teaching: mono-national, non-American students in the UAE; and multi-national, non-American populations in the US. Faculty IS is crucial in today's internationalized tertiary spheres as it affects learning, student belonging, and faculty retention. Data were collected through four-week reflexive participant-generated photography and photo-elicitation interview methods, analyzed using Bennett’s Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity (DMIS). The US-based group exhibited more progressive sensitivity than the UAE-based group, motivating thematic analyses of the DMIS data. Five themes emerged, providing insight into lived experiences and highlighting potential shortcomings of the theoretical framework. This study is the first to the best of the researcher’s knowledge to investigate IS among American faculty teaching internationally diverse populations domestically and to compare IS differences with instructors teaching mono-national, non-American students abroad, offering implications for professionals in internationalized higher education and intercultural research.

latest_articles.title: Sociocultural adaptation in the transnational lives of newcomer migrant adolescents: Digital social networking practices and sociodemographic factors shaping adaptive performance in school and workplace settings
latest_articles.abstract: Navigating cultural boundaries during adolescence, particularly in the digital era, where social media reshapes individual and collective interactions, poses significant challenges for newcomer students. This study, drawing on a sample of 73 participants, examines the extent to which digital networking practices, along with sociodemographic factors, influence sociocultural adaptation, defined here as adaptive performance in school and workplace settings. The findings indicate a positive correlation between adaptive performance and the use of social media for individual learning of the host society’s language ( r= .31, p < .01), as well as for participating in the local culture ( r= .31, p < .01). Multiple regression analysis further reveals that both age ( β =.49, SE =.28, t= 4.50, p < .01) and individual language learning through social networks ( β =.25, SE =.06, t = 2.53, p < . 01) serve as positive predictors of adaptive performance. In contrast, the length of formal education in the home country is identified as a negative predictor ( β = −.319, SE =.67, t= −2.95, p < .01). These results underscore the role of digital platforms as informal learning environments that can enhance sociocultural adaptation. Simultaneously, they challenge the assumption that prolonged formal education in the home country invariably supports adaptation, suggesting that pre-migration educational and pedagogical paradigms may not effectively foster—and might even hinder—the development of adaptive skills in a new cultural milieu.

latest_articles.title: Youth reorientation following forced migration to Norway: Mental health, cultural navigation, and the need for supportive others
latest_articles.abstract: Youth who have experienced conflict, loss, forced displacement, and resettlement may have increased vulnerability to mental health problems. The purpose of this study was to explore how youth with a background as refugees originating from East and Central Africa and the Middle East living in Norway understand mental health and practice self-care strategies. Eighteen youths participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes were developed describing youths’ understanding of mental health, the impact of family and culture, self-care strategies, and reorientation towards mental well-being. Participants described mental health as mood swings, influenced by thoughts, past traumas, current school-related stress, social exclusion, and limited social networks. Additional barriers to improved mental well-being and influence on self-care strategies arose from navigating between cultures and facing conflicting expectations. Some participants described their reorientation processes as meaningful, emphasizing supportive parents, peer-support, new goals, and a sense of meaning as key factors in promoting mental well-being. This study revealed that youths with refugee backgrounds employ both relational and individual strategies for reorientation and self-care, including approaches that emphasize social connection. It is important to include their perspectives to develop culturally safe interventions. Such interventions should incorporate cultural and contextual factors, promote mutual understanding, and strengthen support for newly arrived youth, their families, and those who support them, such as professionals or volunteers.

latest_articles.title: ‘Just interpret’: Navigating trust and ethics in domestic and family violence interpreting
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines Korean–English interpreting in Australian domestic and family violence (DFV) contexts through the lenses of intersectionality and institutional ethnocentrism. Drawing on 17 semi-structured interviews conducted in 2019–2020 and 2024 with National Accreditation Authority for Translators and Interpreters-certified Korean–English interpreters, it explores how practitioners navigate emotional, ethical and professional demands across health, welfare and justice settings. The findings show that limited pre-briefing and inconsistent support increase interpreters’ exposure to vicarious trauma and constrain their ability to prepare adequately for assignments. Trust is negotiated within asymmetrical power relations, where professionals often instruct interpreters to ‘just interpret’, overlooking the linguistic and systemic complexities of interpreting practice. The study argues that interpreting should be treated not as an afterthought but as a strategic component of intercultural communication in DFV practice. It further argues that structural conditions – such as systematic briefings, collaboration, continuity and trauma-informed support – are necessary to enable interpreters to work more ethically and effectively.

latest_articles.title: Human-GenAI Collaboration in Creative Ideation: A Study with Advertising Professionals
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how generative artificial intelligence and prompt quality affect creativity among advertising professionals. Ninety-eight participants were randomly assigned to three conditions: no GenAI, GenAI use, or GenAI use after prompt training. Participants who used GenAI after training generated significantly more ideas than those in the other conditions, although perceived creativity did not differ. Content analysis of prompts revealed key nuances in human–GenAI collaboration. Results underscore the importance of intentionally integrating GenAI to support divergent thinking in creative work.
